title: Multiple Track
context: Grade 4, and the chapter turns round here. An adult sees times tables being recited in another form. What is actually being taught is direction: factors were hunted by closing in on a number and multiples are built by running away from it, and this list has no last entry to find. The second thing being taught is smaller and catches more children, which is that a question asking how many wants a count and not only a list, and that between leaves both of its ends out.

writeup.why: Build the multiples of a number by counting on in equal steps, and find out why the list has no last one.
writeup.look: A track of equal steps running off the right hand edge with a flag on every step, a times table filling in above it and a shaded band below.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Multiple Track' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the steps laid and the flags planted, one number in ink climbing by one as each step goes down, with NO second number beside it and no total to reach, because this is the one tool in the chapter whose list has no length to count towards. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The track runs across the lower half of the working area, a rule 8 tall at 64,520 that starts at a drawn post on the left and carries on through the right hand edge of the frame, where it is neither stopped, nor faded, nor finished with an arrow head: it simply leaves. Each step is drawn exactly as long as every other step, an arc 64 tall laid on the rule, with a numbered flag 48 by 72 planted where it lands, and flags never overlap. The step block sits at the left of the working area, 180 by 180 at 64,286, holding the chosen number as that many countable things so the step has a size and not only a name. The table strip runs above the track, 1086 by 260 at 64,232, one ruled line per flag, filling in as the flags go down so that the table and the track read as one list under two names. Keep going lays step after step and scrolls the track leftwards beneath a fixed frame; a request for the last flag lays the next flag instead and says so, and the track never offers a stopping post. The between band lies under the track, 1086 by 92 at 64,618, carrying two posts that can be dropped anywhere along it. It shades only what lies strictly inside the two posts, and a post landing on a flag leaves that flag fully drawn, at full strength and plainly OUTSIDE the shading, never faded and never covered. Count the band reads out how many flags lie inside it, giving the count first and the names after. Name a flag says which numbered multiple any chosen flag is. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a multiple or a count of them is asked for, and on the fourth phase a small word pad reading between, inside, on the end and how many, so that the question can be answered in words as well as in numbers. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: a number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number built by multiplying is green, anything standing in both lists at once is rose, whatever is left over and any trial that fails is vermilion, the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber, and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome, and every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a trial that failed is told by the leftover standing outside its rows before it is told by a band, and a list that stops is told by the wall at each end of it before it is told by anything else. The right hand edge of the frame is the one measurement in this chapter that must not be tidied. Nothing may be drawn there to round the track off, because a track with an end drawn on it teaches exactly the thing the page teaches by accident every time it prints a table and stops.
writeup.finish: The card shows the longest track the child ran, still leaving the frame with no end mark, and the last band they drew with its count beside it.

phases.win: every flag on the track matches a line of the table, which reads as one list
phases.does: lays several steps and reads the filling table strip beside the flags
phases.goal: the answers of a times table are the multiples of the number
phases.says: Look at the answers in the table. What are you really looking at?
phases.check: Write the table of 12 as far as six lines. What are those six answers called?
phases.feels: the table you already know by heart is the list the chapter is asking for
phases.hands: Say the table of nine aloud the way the class always says it, and write the answers down the side of the board in a column as they come. Then rule a long line under them, step a metre rule along it nine at a time and chalk a mark at every landing. Put the column and the marks beside each other and ask what the two of them have to do with one another. Do the same with the table of twelve.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the answer to that line of the table? Second rung, the phase's: which flag on the track is standing on that number? Third rung: the track is cut to four steps of a small number and the child reads the table strip beside them. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the page asks for the multiples in a line that holds three numbers, and every number in it is a multiple of something, so the instruction really does not say which one is wanted.
wrong.move: rings every number in the line, so that nine and one and eighty-one are all circled as multiples.
wrong.screen: the line is read out as so many steps of nine, and the track lays exactly that many steps beside it. Only the place the steps land carries a flag; the step size and the number of steps are drawn on the step block and on the arcs instead, where neither of them is a flag. The child's rings stay exactly where they were put and the flag that the line names lights beside them.

wrong.why: both words are about one number and its friends, both arrive out of multiplication, and nothing in the sound of either says which way the list is supposed to run.
wrong.move: reads the column of answers as the factors of nine, because the two words turned up in the same week.
wrong.screen: the pen from the topic before opens under the track holding the factors of nine, one and three and nine, penned between its two posts with both walls drawn. Above it the track runs its flags out through the edge of the frame with no end mark. The two are left on the stage together and read out one after the other, the short shut list and the one that leaves.

phases.screen: an empty track with the step block set and the table strip blank
phases.soWhat: The answers in a times table are the multiples of that number.
phases.concept: A times table read as a list

phases.win: the first flag lands on the number itself and the table strip shows one times it
phases.does: lays the first step and reads where the flag lands
phases.goal: the first multiple of a number is the number itself
phases.says: Lay one step only. Which number are you standing on now?
phases.check: What is the lowest multiple of 18, and what is its lowest factor? Say why those two answers are different.
phases.feels: the first step you lay lands on the number you started from
phases.hands: Chalk a start line and have a child take exactly one stride of twenty-three centimetres along a metre rule. Ask which number they are standing on, before anybody works anything out. Write the first line of the table of twenty-three under it. Then ask for the lowest multiple of eighteen and the lowest factor of eighteen in the same breath, and write the two answers side by side.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many steps have been laid so far? Second rung, the phase's: where did that one step land? Third rung: the track is cleared and the child lays the first step of a small number and reads the flag. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: counting on sounds like moving away from where you are, so the place the counting started from does not feel like one of the places it reached.
wrong.move: starts the list at twice the number, leaving the number itself off the front of it.
wrong.screen: one step is laid, one flag is planted, and the flag lands on the number itself with the first line of the table strip writing itself above it, one step of it. The child's list stays exactly where it was written, and the missing first entry is drawn as an empty flag standing in front of it.

wrong.why: lowest has meant the smallest number in sight all year, and one is the smallest number that turns up in any of this chapter's lists.
wrong.move: answers lowest multiple with one, because one is the lowest factor of everything.
wrong.screen: the pen and the track are drawn one above the other for the same number, with the one card lying inside the pen against its left post and no flag anywhere on the track standing on one. The first flag lights instead, and the two lists are read out in turn, the one that starts at one and the one that starts at the number.

phases.screen: the track cleared with only the first step waiting to be laid
phases.soWhat: The first and lowest multiple of a number is the number itself.
phases.concept: The first multiple of a number

phases.win: the track scrolls on with no end mark and the child says out loud that there is no last one
phases.does: asks for the last flag and is handed the next one instead, over and over
phases.goal: there is no last multiple, because the next step is always there
phases.says: Show me the last one. Can you? What happens every time you try?
phases.check: Write down the greatest multiple of 6 that you can. Now say what is wrong with the question.
phases.feels: every time you ask for the last one you are handed the next one
phases.hands: Write the multiples of fifteen along a strip of paper, fifteen, thirty, forty-five, sixty, and keep going until the strip runs out. Then stick another strip on the end and carry on. Ask for the greatest multiple of six anybody in the room can write, let somebody write it, and then add six to it in front of them. Ask what is wrong with the question rather than with the answer.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which flag is standing at the end of the track so far? Second rung, the phase's: what happens if you lay one more step? Third rung: the track is cut short, the child asks for the last flag three times over, and three new flags arrive. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: every written table stops somewhere and the page is where the child meets one, so the page itself keeps teaching the opposite of what the chapter is claiming.
wrong.move: writes down the last number on the page and calls it the last multiple.
wrong.screen: the track runs on past where the child stopped, one step at a time and each exactly as long as the last, and the table strip writes one more line for each. The number the child wrote down keeps its flag and its place in the run, with the steps carrying on past it and out through the edge of the frame.

wrong.why: the tables that were learnt end at ten or twelve lines, and a list that has always ended in the same place looks like a list with an end.
wrong.move: says the multiples run out somewhere past a hundred, because that is where the tables stop.
wrong.screen: keep going is left running and the track scrolls past a hundred, then past several hundred, then past a thousand, with the step block untouched in the corner and each arc drawn exactly the same length as the first one. The flag the child named keeps its own mark, far back down the track, and the edge of the frame stays as empty as it was.

phases.screen: a long track already scrolling with no end mark drawn
phases.soWhat: A number has infinite multiples, so there is no last one to find.

phases.win: the flags on the posts stay drawn outside the shading and the band reads out its count
phases.does: drops the posts, shades the middle and counts what is strictly inside
phases.goal: a multiple sitting on either post is not inside the band
phases.says: Count only what is inside the band. What about the two on the posts?
phases.check: How many multiples of 8 lie between 39 and 70, and what are they? Give the count first.
phases.feels: the two flags on the posts are drawn as plainly as ever, and neither one is inside
phases.hands: Peg a washing line across the room and hang number cards on it for the multiples of seven. Give two children a ribbon each and send them to stand at twenty-eight and at fifty-six. Ask the class to count the cards between the ribbons, and then ask whether the two cards the ribbons are touching are between them or not. Write the answer on the board as a number first and a list second.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which flags are standing on the two posts? Second rung, the phase's: is a flag on a post inside the band or outside it? Third rung: the band is cut to a short stretch of a small step and the child counts the flags in it with a finger. The word pad stays open.

wrong.why: both ends really are multiples, so they look as though they belong in the answer, and between is heard as everything from here to there.
wrong.move: counts twenty-eight and fifty-six in, because both of them are multiples of seven too.
wrong.screen: the two posts are dropped exactly on those two flags and both flags stay fully drawn at full strength. Only the stretch strictly inside the posts is shaded, and the shading stops short of each post so the gap between the shading and the flag is visible. The band then counts what it holds, and the child's answer stays in the slot beside it.

wrong.why: the numbers are the work that was done and the question is about them, so saying them feels like a complete answer, and the chapter's own worked example answers this very question with a list and stops.
wrong.move: answers how many multiples by naming them and never gives a number.
wrong.screen: the question is read again with the words how many lit, and the flags inside the band are counted out one at a time with the count standing in the corner and going up as each is touched. The list the child gave stays exactly where it was written and the count is drawn above it, so both answers are on the stage together.

phases.screen: the track with a band whose two posts both land on flags
phases.soWhat: Between leaves out both ends, and a how many question wants the count as well as the list.

writeup.delight: The third phase, when the last one is asked for. The track does not refuse and nothing is marked: it simply lays one more step of exactly the same length, plants one more numbered flag, writes one more line into the table strip, and scrolls so that the new flag is in the frame and the edge is empty again. Ask again and it happens again, at the same pace, with the step length never changing by a hair. A child can sit there asking for the last one as long as they like, and the only thing that ever comes back is the next one, which is the whole answer to the question and is never said out loud.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the step block is set, the track is empty and the table strip above it is ruled and blank. On the second the track is cleared back to the start post with one step waiting to be laid and nothing beyond it. On the third the track is already long, running out through the right hand edge of the frame with no end mark on it and no last step drawn. On the fourth the track is long and flagged and the between band lies under it with both of its posts standing on flags and nothing shaded yet. The running count at the top left holds the steps laid and the flags planted, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first blank line of the table strip, or the single step waiting at the start, or the edge of the frame where the track leaves it, or the left hand post of the band, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks where the next step is going to land. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any step size, the track run as far as the child cares to, with the table strip and the between band on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on reading a table as a list, naming a first or a numbered multiple, saying why the list has no end, and counting the multiples inside a band.
voiceLines: A track, one step block, and no end mark anywhere along it.
Look at the answers in the table. What are you really looking at?
Lay one step only. Which number are you standing on now?
Show me the last one. Can you? What happens every time you try?
Count only what is inside the band. What about the two on the posts?
A new step size. Where is the very first step going to land?
Free play. Any step size, the track as far as you like, the band on or off.
Lay the steps again one at a time and read the table filling beside them.
Still running off the edge, and you never did find a last one.

observations.why: A multiple is the number multiplied by a whole number, and that is what each line of the table already says.
observations.soWhat: The multiples are the table the child has known by heart all year, under a new name.
observations.observe: Every line of the times table matched a flag on the track, one for one.

observations.why: One step of the number is the number, which is the first line of its own table.
observations.soWhat: The first and lowest multiple of a number is the number itself.
observations.observe: The very first step landed on the number itself.

observations.why: Whatever multiple you stop at, multiplying by the next whole number gives another.
observations.soWhat: The list of multiples has no last entry, so it cannot be counted the way a factor list can.
observations.observe: Asking for the last flag never produced one; it produced the next flag.

observations.why: Between means strictly inside the two ends, so an end is a boundary and not a member.
observations.soWhat: Both ends are left out, and the count is what a how many question is asking for.
observations.observe: A flag standing on a post was drawn as plainly as any other and still sat outside the shading.

description: Step a number along a track that never reaches an end, and band a stretch of it to see what between leaves out.

source_tool.description: A track runs left to right across the stage and off the right hand edge, with no end mark and no last step ever drawn. A step block the size of the chosen number sits at the start, and each tap lays another step of exactly the same size, with a flag planted where it lands. The first flag falls on the number itself, which is the point of the first phase. A table strip above the track fills in as the flags go down, so the answers of a times table and the flags on the track are shown to be one list under two names. A keep going control lays step after step and the track scrolls without ever offering a stopping post; asking for the last one returns the next one instead. Below the track sits a between band with two posts that can be dropped anywhere. The band shades only what lies strictly inside it, and a post that lands on a flag keeps that flag drawn and plainly OUTSIDE the shading, which is what makes the two ends visible rather than argued about. A count control reads out how many flags the band holds as well as naming them.
source_tool.art_direction: A flagged track that leaves the frame / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: trays of countable things, ruled rows on a board, a ladder of rungs with one trial to a rung, a pen with a wall at each end, a track of equal steps, cards that turn over, and two rings of cord that overlap.

Equal groups are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a row is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are in it, and the rows are kept apart by a drawn wall or a plain gap and never by colour alone.

Whatever is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the rows, on the same surface, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never crossed out, never tucked under a row and never left to be guessed from a gap. The leftover is the reason a trial failed, so it is the last thing any stage may hide.

A list of factors is drawn penned in between one and the number itself, with both ends of the run plainly stopped by a wall or a final post, so the list can be seen to end. A list of multiples is drawn running from the number away to the right, and the track carrying it leaves the frame with no end mark and no last step drawn, so the list can be seen not to end. The two never run the same way on one stage.

A run of trials is drawn unbroken. Every whole number from one up to the last one tried keeps its own rung or row, in order, with none left out, and a trial that fails is drawn and marked as a failure rather than dropped.
Where the digits of a number are added, every digit sits in its own cell, zeros included, and a cell holding a zero is drawn and counted in rather than left out of the line.
Nothing the child is asked to count one at a time comes to more than twenty things in one group. A larger quantity is a ruled array of identical tiles or a written numeral, never a loose heap.
A list is told apart by the wall or the open edge at its end first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a number, a counter or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. A number that divides another exactly is deep blue, a number that is built by multiplying is green, and anything standing in both lists at once is rose, and those three hold in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Whatever is left over, and any trial that fails, is vermilion; the number being broken up or the total in hand is amber; and a single digit being read or added is sky blue. All of that holds in greyscale, because a failed trial is told apart by the leftover drawn outside its row before it is told apart by colour, and a factor list is told apart from a list of multiples by the wall at each end of it before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Lay the steps again one at a time and read the table filling beside them.
voice.onNext: A new step size. Where is the very first step going to land?
voice.opening: A track, one step block, and no end mark anywhere along it.
voice.onFinish: Still running off the edge, and you never did find a last one.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any step size, the track as far as you like, the band on or off.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: A times table read as a list
The first multiple of a number

placement.where: Right after a times table has been said aloud and written down by hand. The tool is what runs the list off the edge of the frame with no last step drawn, which a written table cannot do because a written table always stops somewhere.

answer_key.rule: A multiple of a number is that number multiplied by a whole number, so the answers in its times table are its multiples. The first multiple of any number is the number itself, because one times it is it, so every counting number is a multiple of itself and is its own lowest multiple. The list never runs out: whatever multiple you stop at, the next whole number gives another, so a number has infinite multiples. Between two numbers means strictly inside them, so a multiple sitting on either end is not counted. Answer a how many question with the count as well as the list.
answer_key.wrong: The steps are laid again one at a time at walking pace with the table strip filling in beside them, and the band is redrawn with its posts lit so that a flag standing on a post can be seen to be outside the shading. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: One nine is 9, two nines are 18, three nines are 27, and the steps are all the same size.
Every answer is 9 multiplied by a whole number, so every answer is a multiple of 9.
items.answer: 9, 18, 27, 36, 45 and 54, and they are the multiples of 9
items.question: Write the first six answers in the table of 9. What is that list called?
items.checkpoint: The answers in a times table are the multiples of that number.
items.misconception: Thinking multiples are a new thing to learn rather than the table already known by heart.

steps: The first step laid on the track is one step long, and it lands on 23.
1 times 23 is 23, which is the first line of its table.
That holds for every number, so every counting number is a multiple of itself.
items.question: What is the first multiple of 23, and how do you know?
items.checkpoint: The first multiple of a number is always the number itself.
items.misconception: Starting the list at twice the number, because the number itself looks too easy to count.

steps: The twelfth multiple is 132, because 11 times 12 is 132.
Multiplying by the next whole number gives 143, and then it goes on again.
Whatever multiple you stop at, there is always another, so 11 has infinite multiples.
items.answer: No. There is no last one
items.question: You have written twelve multiples of 11. Can you write the last one?
items.checkpoint: Multiples never run out, which is the opposite of factors, and they do run out.
items.misconception: Treating the last multiple written down as the end of the list, because the page stopped there.

steps: The multiples of 9 run 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63 and on.
18 and 63 are multiples of 9 as well, but between means strictly inside, so both are left out.
That leaves 27, 36, 45 and 54, which is four of them, and the count is part of the answer.
items.question: How many multiples of 9 lie between 18 and 63, and what are they?
items.checkpoint: Between leaves out both ends, and a how many question wants the count as well as the list.
items.misconception: Counting 18 and 63 in because they are multiples too, which makes six instead of four.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: Write the first five multiples of 13.
What is the first multiple of 37?
Continue the pattern 11, 22, 33 with the next three multiples.
Which is the lowest multiple of 23, and which is its third multiple?
items.final_answer: 23 is the lowest, and the third is 69

items.question: A child says the multiples of 20 stop at 100. What would you tell the child?
items.final_answer: That they do not stop. 20 times 6 is 120, and there is always a next one after that

items.question: Write every multiple of 6 that lies between 25 and 55.
How many factors has 51, and how many multiples?
items.final_answer: Four factors, 1, 3, 17 and 51, and its multiples never run out

items.question: How many multiples of 11 lie between 22 and 88, and what are they?
items.final_answer: Five of them: 33, 44, 55, 66 and 77. The two ends are multiples of 11 as well, but between leaves them out

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: sets the size of the step, which is the number being counted on
lays one more step of the same size and plants a flag where it lands
fills in the times table above the track as the flags go down
lays step after step and scrolls, offering no stopping post
drops two posts and shades only what lies strictly inside them
reads out how many flags the band holds, as well as naming them
says which numbered multiple a chosen flag is

teaching_notes: Say a times table aloud before the tool is opened and write the answers in a column, then open the track and let the class see that the column and the flags are the same list. That saves multiples from arriving as a new word for something nobody knew. Spend real time on the first step, because the first multiple of a number being the number itself sounds like a trick and is used later in two places, for the lowest multiple of a number and for the fact that a number stands at both ends of its own two lists. Then run the keep going control until somebody asks you to stop, and ask them why you cannot. Hold that answer against the pen from the topic before, where the list shut at both ends: one runs out and the other does not, and that is the only place where the two words genuinely differ. The between band deserves the last quarter of the session. Put both posts on flags on purpose, ask for the count before the list, and keep asking for the count, because the chapter's own worked example answers a how many question with three numbers and never says three.
generation_prompt: Build a multiples tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A horizontal track runs left to right and leaves the frame at the right hand edge with no end mark and no final step ever drawn. A step block sets the size of one step, and each tap lays one more step of exactly that length with a numbered flag planted where it lands, the first flag falling on the number itself. A times table strip above the track fills in one line per flag, so the table and the flags visibly read as one list. A keep going control lays steps continuously and scrolls the track; a request for the last flag returns the next flag instead, with the track never offering an end post. Below the track a between band carries two draggable posts and shades only the stretch strictly inside them; a post landing on a flag keeps that flag fully drawn and plainly outside the shaded region, never faded and never covered. A count control reads out how many flags lie inside the band and names them, giving the count first. A name a flag control says which numbered multiple any chosen flag is. Steps are always drawn exactly equal in length and flags never overlap. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Set the step to your number. Lay one step and see where the flag lands. Keep laying steps and watch the table fill in beside them. Try to find the last one. Then drop the band and count only the flags inside it.
